title: Childcare delivery changes the economic and social returns of informal-sector women’s work
source_unit: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11442, Childcare for Informal-Sector Workers: Delivery Models, Access, and Welfare, September 2026
geography: Kampala, Uganda; 883 women market vendors across six markets, their children, household caregivers, community childcare providers, and workplace-based childcare services

denominator.unit: women market vendors randomized to free workplace- or community-based childcare in six Kampala-area markets

care_distribution.value: free childcare redistributes caregiving away from household members

women_earnings.value: free childcare raises women’s hourly earnings

observations.method: Randomized controlled trial comparing free childcare access and workplace-based versus community-based delivery among women market vendors.
observations.uncertainty: The causal estimates are specific to participating market vendors, children, services, and implementation conditions in Kampala; they do not establish identical effects for other informal occupations or locations.
observations.subgroup: Women informal workers, children needing care, household members who provide unpaid care, and vendors with different work locations, earnings, and family support.
observations.counterinterpretation: Childcare can release women’s time and improve productivity, but care quality, safety, affordability after subsidy, and children’s needs determine whether economic gains are durable.

community_model.value: community centers achieve higher utilization and larger gains in child development and women’s well-being

workplace_model.value: workplace centers generate larger economic impacts

marginal_value.value: both models have high marginal value of public funds

observations.method: Randomized comparison of workplace-based childcare corners and community-based private childcare centers, with utilization, child, well-being, and economic outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison does not imply that one model dominates universally; utilization, proximity, quality, operating hours, labour-market structure, and scale can change relative performance.
observations.subgroup: Women who work at markets, children with different care needs, households relying on relatives, and communities with different proximity to childcare facilities.
observations.counterinterpretation: A workplace model may be economically powerful where care and work are co-located, while community provision may be more adaptable to irregular schedules and broader household use.

observations.period: 2023-2026; care, productivity, and household welfare mechanism

denominator.unit: informal-sector women workers in Kampala childcare trial

care_constraint.value: childcare burdens are identified as a productivity constraint for women in informal work

welfare_set.value: the study connects childcare access to women’s earnings, child development, and women’s well-being

design_question.value: the study addresses how childcare support should be structured, not simply whether it exists

observations.method: Randomized evaluation of childcare access and delivery design among informal-sector women workers.
observations.uncertainty: The trial does not establish long-run labour formalisation, fertility, household bargaining, provider sustainability without subsidy, or general equilibrium effects on informal markets.
observations.subgroup: Women vendors, children, spouses and relatives providing care, informal employers and market authorities, and childcare workers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Childcare provision may improve household welfare without changing gender norms or labour-market segmentation; economic gains can coexist with continued unequal responsibility for care.

boundary: This record adds a causal childcare-to-informal-work route linking care redistribution, women’s earnings, child development, well-being, utilization, delivery model, and public value. It does not establish long-run formalisation, fertility, universal delivery superiority, provider sustainability without subsidy, or general equilibrium effects beyond the Kampala trial.
